metadata.title: Conversation with Vincent Koc: OpenClaw's Reflections and Evolution, China's 'Lobster' Craze, and the Next Step for Agents
metadata.guest_role: Chief Architect, OpenClaw Foundation · Core maintainer of the open-source agent framework

conclusion: OpenClaw Foundation chief architect Vincent Koc, at WIC 2026 Shanghai, traces OpenClaw from Peter Steinberger's experiment to a global craze: February SF lines around the block, China's 'lobster' install wave outpacing Silicon Valley, npm weekly downloads above 4M after Q1 hype cooled. Unlike Codex-style coding assistants, it is a personal agent that modifies its own code — always-on Gateway, heartbeat, skills/MCP. As a 501(c)(3) 'Switzerland for AI agents,' a five-person core team uses agent-first factories to survive 13k PRs. Next unlocks: agent interoperability, containerized security, and personal AI for everyone.
background: Silicon Valley 101 sits down with Vincent Koc at the 2026 World AI Conference in Shanghai. He discovered OpenClaw on X in December 2024, became a maintainer in January, and lived through its arc from developer toy to enterprise deploy, China's nationwide 'lobster raising,' and foundation governance. Context includes Peter Steinberger donating the project to a nonprofit and joining OpenAI, Chinese tech giants shipping Qclaw/Wu/Dclaw derivatives, and post-Claw competitors like Manus and Hermes.
important_facts: China vs West adoption: Chinese employees got KPIs to automate tasks with OpenClaw and embraced it fast; Western enterprises often blocked it first over security. Codex/Claude Code are hard to use in China, so locally deployable open source became a catalyst. Tencent WorkBuddy and newer agents aren't built on OpenClaw code but support its skills framework — Koc calls this the 'postclaw era,' where ecosystem beats a single product.

Architecture and scale: Gateway is an always-on hub linking messaging channels, models, memory, and tools; heartbeat triggers background work every 10–30 minutes. Sessions moved from flat files to a database so enterprises can swap in real DB clusters. Peak ~13,000 open PRs forced custom AI agent review and a 'factory' test stack (any OS/cloud in ~20 seconds, screenshot/video proof). Nearly 100 ecosystem repos, each like its own startup.

Foundation governance and roadmap: 501(c)(3) nonprofit, donation-funded hiring; mission to empower humanity with AI and be neutral 'Switzerland.' No direct consumer hosting — instead enabling Microsoft Scout forks and internal enterprise builds. Memory, multi-tenancy, and long-horizon tasks remain unsolved; default single-agent is enough for most users, with specialists split like managing employees. Next 12 months: agent-to-agent communication is the big unlock; computer-use models fill API gaps.

mental_model.name: Personal Agent × Open Swiss × Agent-First Factory
mental_model.components: Treat OpenClaw as a personal employee that can rewrite its own code, not a turn-based coding assistant; Gateway + skills + MCP form an extensible harness. Foundation status buys global trust (especially China) and ecosystem forks; scale comes from agents engineering their own test/review pipelines, not headcount.
mental_model.application: Diligence agent frameworks on always-on behavior, self-modification, Day-0 multi-model support, and enterprise backends. OpenClaw itself is nonprofit, but token usage, computer-use, and security containerization benefit model/API vendors. Enterprise deploys should prioritize container boundaries plus auto-approval modes; China scenarios need compliance and local models post-trained on OpenClaw.

key_insights.view: After hype cooled, real adoption accelerated.
key_insights.question: What happened post-Q1?
key_insights.answer: Early agent-first development caused stability issues and uninstalls; after fixes, npm weekly downloads rose from ~2.5–3M pre-hype to 4M+. Koc sees the cooldown as healthy — focus shifted to reliable software and factory tooling, not virality.

key_insights.question: How is it different from Codex?
key_insights.answer: Coding agents write code inside a fixed harness; OpenClaw learns memory, builds skills, and changes its own code for new models/APIs — groceries, new lab model support, self-evolution. The difference: the agent can modify itself.

key_insights.view: Foundation status is survival and fairness.
key_insights.question: Why not commercialize?
key_insights.answer: Peter insisted on an independent foundation, not single-company or country control, so China, US tech, and everyday users all embrace it. Koc says partners reach out precisely because of foundation neutrality — trading equity upside for industry positive-sum.

top_investment_implications.thesis: Open-source personal/enterprise agent harness — Gateway, skills ecosystem, Day-0 multi-model, foundation governance; npm downloads and global adoption validate PMF. Nonprofit limits direct monetization but shapes agent interoperability and skill standards
